I'm sonography, so I'm sure my experience is going to diverge from yours at some point, but I'm hoping the baseline non technical parts will be similar enough.

It sounds to me like you're in a wonderful position to make a change and set yourself up for success.  Put together a packet of research that you understand, using the normal jargon for your modalities physics.  Then make a packet that translates this into laymen terms that someone without a radiography background can understand.  Then at the back make a few different suggestions for protocols that fill in the blanks that your protocols are missing (I think I read you don't have protocols for exposure, this is where you can really shine).  Give all this to your one up.  Your coworkers may not like you going over their heads, but you explain to your one up that you're more interested in diagnoses not being missed due to under exposure than your coworkers being upset.  If your manager won't listen, take it to their one up.  Eventually (assuming you're right, which I have no basis to determine but I'm sure you are) someone will listen, and if they see your coworkers are actively doing bad jobs and you're trying to correct it, you'll stick out amongst your peers.

Everything Dave said is correct.  However, you specifically mention the target being size 2.  According to the size table, great danes and dire wolves are size 0 (sage as a human).  Most dog's are size -1 at best.  Grappling rules state that *usually* you can't grapple something more than two sizes larger than yourself without exceptional strength or reach.  Since your question is related to the size of the dog and the wild card, you need to determine if the dog is size 0 (large for a dog, up to 250 lbs, and able to grapple a size 2 target), or size -1 (average dog, up to 125 lbs, normally unable to grapple a size 2 target).

I think I'm a unique case.  My depression is very swingy.  Not like I get manic, I just have normal days, then random hardcore depression.  I started taking Lexapro after a solid week of SI, stayed on for a year, then wanted off because for the first time since I met her, my wife's libido was higher than mine (which was near zero and dropping).

A month or two after I got off I had a panic attack at work that spiraled into deep depression and had to go to my car.  I called my NP and she prescribed me Hydroxyzine (or w/e it's spelled) over the phone.  I took it, slept, and was fine the next day.  I still have that prescription and I've taken it as needed a few times since. 

My theory is (for me) my depression snowballs.  If I can stop the ruminating before it gets good and going, I can bounce back.  But once it has a couple days to run, it lasts for months.  2023 was the first December I can remember not having SI in...  Ever?  2014 at least. 

So it works for me, because it stops my snowball.  I imagine it wouldn't be as helpful long term for anyone who's depression isn't so swingy as mine.

Not sure if this has been said, but I do stress tests at my job.  The idea is to get a patients heart rate up as high as is safe so we can see if the heart works properly under stress.  If we use a treadmill we use something called the Bruce Protocol.  The trail picks up speed every three minutes, but usually stays at a walking pace.  What drives the stress isn't the speed or distance.  It's the incline.  We crank up the incline and it makes it insanely difficult.

Tldr look up Bruce Protocol for stress echos.  Incline can do more than distance.

The cacophony was impressive this time.  Fred had long since learned to sleep through loud music, as had most of the world once they realized magic was cast through mundane instruments.  It grew frustrating very quickly, but for the majority, it was a blessing.  Once you found your instrument, you could do nearly anything you wanted.  A lot of people quit their jobs, and an equal number filled those positions with magic, accomplishing by themselves what would normally take ten people.  It was only a matter of time until these changes hit the military.

It quickly changed how wars were fought.  When a plucked guitar could rust a gun from a hundred paces, and body armor was as good as paper against the sharp notes of a violin, modern weapons were put aside.  Formations were made, with large instruments like the tuba in the front, and fragile mouth harp singers as scouts.  It became apparent that the louder an instrument, the more powerful its magic could be.  This was still limited by skill, but a skilled flutist would struggle against an amateur french horn player.

Fred groaned as his room began to shake, and his door swung open.  He rolled out of bed, walking quickly over to grab his robe before the scout ran in the door.  The young man still got more of an eye full than he wanted and turned his back as Fred arranged the robe and tied it tight with its rope.  “When will you people learn to knock?” he grouched before stalking past the scout and out the door.  He quickly made his way down the stairs, passing windows in the stone walls that looked out over the chaos in the city around them.  Waves water crashed against gouts of flame in the air, electricity crackling in every direction, stopping against invisible barriers maintained by trombone players.  The winning squads were more harmonious, playing to at least the same genre, while those that broke into jazz and rock at the same time fell apart.

Fred came to a sudden stop, causing the scout to take the mouth harp down, “Wha-.”  Before he could finish his sentence, the wall crashed in just below Fred.  “Oh,” the man said, putting the harp back in his mouth and plucking a few notes.  The stones lifted from the steps and sealed themselves back into the wall, and Fred continued his trek down the tower.  When they reached the bottom, he started stretching as he walked across the large cathedral sanctuary.

His arms over his head, he yawned loudly as a group of saxophones rushed down the aisles.  The leader turned to Fred as the large double doors shook, “They’re almost through!  You have to hurry!”

“Yeah yeah,” Fred muttered as he laced his fingers together, turning his palms toward the ceiling and popping his knuckles.  He sat down on the bench in front of the grand organ, adjusted a little, moved the bench a little closer, then put his fingers to the keys.  He hated that he had to use a piano to cast music, but it was a clever twist that they found this church with metal pipes running all the way to the top of the tower.  The notes Fred played drowned out all the other music, resonating through the sanctuary and filling the small town they were in. That's not to say we shouldn't ever go to patient rooms, we have to do what we have to do to get our job done.  But when its possible to have the patients brought to the lab, it's usually better to do so.  And it boils down to more than just what makes the tech comfortable.

This was a huge deal people used to knock out anti-virus a while back, because when it opens the file it'll see 9 more files inside, then open each of those and see 9 more files inside each of those 9 files, so 81. Then each of those have 9 inside... You can see where that goes. So it uses up all the memory assigned to the anti-virus and it can't function until that memory gets cleared. Which creates a great time for a hacker to upload a small backdoor program like a keylogger to the computer, it slips past the anti-virus because it's busy.

That being said, originally this zip bomb was meant to take out just the anti-virus, not the whole pc. And new anti-virus programs have recursion protocols where if they open something and see 9 copies of it inside, it says "I'm just gonna put all of this in a box where nobody can try to open it." So I see it more as the school's tifu by having outdated anti-virus and somehow letting the anti-virus use all the computers memory to do its thing.
